title: One-time code by text
like: the login code text that arrives in seconds
brief: Apps ask you to send a six-digit code to a phone. The code must arrive in seconds, a person must never get it twice, and nobody may use your system to spam a number. Texts go through a carrier partner with a hard speed limit and a real price per message.

clarify.q: How fast must the code arrive?
clarify.a: Within about 10 seconds of the request. Late codes are as bad as none.

clarify.q: Can the same request be sent twice?
clarify.a: Apps retry when they are unsure. Send each code only once.
Limit how many codes one phone number can get in a few minutes.

notes: The carrier partner accepts about 100 texts a second per sender in this scenario (approx.).
Each text costs about a cent (approx.). Every code is a real bill.

numbers.label: Codes to send per second at peak
Texts a day
numbers.how: Average load is about 0.45 of peak: 8 × 0.45 × 86,400 ≈ 310,000 (approx.)

numbers.label: Text bill a month
numbers.how: 310,000 × 30 × about $0.008 ≈ $75,000 (approx.). This is why abuse limits matter.

hints: The carrier has a speed limit and a code that arrives late is useless. What smooths a burst without delaying everyone?
Put a queue before the carrier. Use an idempotency store so a retry never sends a second text, and a rate limiter per phone number.
Load balancer, servers, rate limiter, a key-value store for codes, queue, workers with an idempotency store, the text provider, and a dead-letter queue.

editorial.summary: Accept the request quickly, limit abuse per number, and put the send in a queue. Workers check that the code has not been sent already and hand it to the carrier at the speed it allows.

designs.name: Rate limit, queue, one send per code
designs.why: The limiter stops number spam before it costs money. The queue smooths bursts to the carrier limit. The idempotency check makes an app retry harmless.

tradeoffs: A queue can delay a code when the carrier slows. Giving codes their own queue keeps marketing texts from waiting in the same line.
Strict per-number limits stop abuse but may block a real person who retries a few times.
A second carrier partner raises uptime, at the price of another contract and another limit to respect.
Sending the code by email or an authenticator app is far cheaper than texting every time.
editorial.realWorld: Code texts cost roughly a cent or two each, so even a modest app pays a large bill, and carriers cap their speed, so large apps rate limit hard and often offer an authenticator app instead (approx.).
